# QM Intermediate Code Sheet {#intermediate-code-sheet}

This sheet collects the R commands and formulas of QM Intermediate, ordered
by lecture. The names `y`, `x`, `group`, and `df` are placeholders. Replace
them by the variables and the dataset of the exam question.

The code sheet is provided at the exam. The table shows which sections you
need when.

| When | Sections to use |
|---|---|
| Tutorial 1 | Workflow and Lectures 1--3 |
| Tutorial 2 | Complete sheet, Lectures 1--6 |
| Final exam (in TestVision) | Complete sheet, Lectures 1--6 |

The sheet helps with R syntax and with calculations. You must still define
the sample, check the assumptions, interpret units and reference categories,
and tell association from causation.

::: {.formula-sheet}

## Workflow and data checks

```r
df <- read.csv("data.csv")

dim(df)
names(df)
head(df)
str(df)
summary(df)
colSums(is.na(df))
table(df$group, useNA = "ifany")
```

Create new variables in visible code. Put money in readable units (this
course uses millions or thousands of dollars). When you compare models, fit them all on the same
observations:

```r
df$x_1k <- df$x_euros / 1000
df$group <- factor(df$group)
df$group <- relevel(df$group, ref = "reference")

needed <- c("y", "x1", "x2", "group")
analysis <- df[complete.cases(df[needed]), ]
```

For every exam analysis:

1. Say what one row is, and name the outcome, the predictors, their units,
   and the sample.
2. Inspect the values and check for missing values.
3. Make a graph that fits the variables.
4. Fit the model and check its diagnostics.
5. Report the estimates, their uncertainty, the fit, and the relevant test.
6. Interpret the results in context, and state the limits that come from
   the sample and the reasons why a result is or is not causal.

## Lecture 1: Simple linear regression

The population model and fitted line are

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\widehat Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_i.
$$

For simple OLS,

$$
\hat\beta_1=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}
{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}
=\frac{s_{XY}}{s_X^2}
=r_{XY}\,\frac{s_Y}{s_X},
\qquad
\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.
$$

The residual and least-squares criterion are

$$
e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{SSE}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2.
$$

Fit and inspect a simple regression:

```r
m <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
coef(m)
summary(m)

fitted(m)
residuals(m)
```

Plot the observations and fitted line:

```r
plot(y ~ x, data = df,
     xlab = "Predictor (unit)", ylab = "Outcome (unit)")
abline(m, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
```

Calculate a fitted value or ask R for fitted conditional means:

```r
b <- coef(m)
b[1] + b[2] * x0

new_cases <- data.frame(x = c(x0, x1))
predict(m, newdata = new_cases)
predict(m, newdata = new_cases, interval = "confidence")
```

Interpret $\hat\beta_1$ as the fitted change in the outcome for a one-unit
increase in the predictor. State both units, and write "associated with"
unless the data come from an experiment. Rescaling both variables by the
same factor changes the intercept and leaves the slope unchanged.
Multiplying only the outcome by a factor multiplies the slope by it.
Multiplying only the predictor by a factor divides the slope by it (see the
worked example on units in Lecture 1).

## Lecture 2: Assumptions, residual diagnostics, and influence

The diagnostic plots check the assumptions in the table of Lecture 2. A
curve in the residual plot puts the linear conditional mean in doubt. A fan
shape puts the constant conditional variance in doubt. Large standardised
residuals or large Cook's distances flag observations that you must
investigate. Plots cannot show independence, the absence of confounding,
the quality of the measurement, or causality. These depend on how the data
were collected.

Make the two main diagnostic plots:

```r
plot(fitted(m), residuals(m),
     xlab = "Fitted value", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

qqnorm(rstandard(m))
qqline(rstandard(m))
```

Find unusual and influential observations. Lecture 2 explains the first five
commands (`nobs(m)` is the number of observations $n$). The three
`plot(m, which = ...)` lines are shortcuts that draw the residual plot, the
Q--Q plot, and a plot of Cook's distance:

```r
summary(residuals(m))         # summary of the residuals, a first check
rstandard(m)                  # standardised residuals, beyond about ±3 is large
cooks.distance(m)             # influence, a common threshold is 4/n
sum(abs(rstandard(m)) > 3)
sum(cooks.distance(m) > 4 / nobs(m))

plot(m, which = 1)  # residuals versus fitted
plot(m, which = 2)  # normal Q--Q
plot(m, which = 4)  # Cook's distance
```

For a flagged observation: investigate it and report it. Never delete it
without reporting.

## Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test

For a two-sided test against zero,

$$
H_0:\beta_j=0,
\qquad
H_1:\beta_j\ne0,
\qquad
t=\frac{\hat\beta_j}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\beta_j)}.
$$

With $k$ slopes and an intercept, the residual degrees of freedom and the
95% confidence interval are

$$
df=n-k-1,
\qquad
\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,\,df}\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\beta_j).
$$

In simple regression, $k=1$ and $df=n-2$. The multiplier $t_{0.975,\,df}$
is `qt(0.975, df)` in R.

```r
summary(m)                 # estimates, SEs, t tests, p-values, fit
confint(m, level = 0.95)   # coefficient confidence intervals
df.residual(m)
nobs(m)
qt(0.975, df.residual(m))  # multiplier for a 95% interval
```

To verify R's two-sided test against zero:

```r
tab <- summary(m)$coefficients
t_value <- tab["x", "Estimate"] / tab["x", "Std. Error"]
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = df.residual(m))
```

The decomposition of variation:

$$
\text{SST}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2,\qquad
\text{SSE}=\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2,\qquad
\text{SSR}=\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2,
$$

$$
\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE},
\qquad
R^2=1-\frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}
=\frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}}.
$$

Calculate the components:

```r
y <- model.response(model.frame(m))
yhat <- fitted(m)

SST <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
SSE <- sum(residuals(m)^2)
SSR <- SST - SSE
R2 <- 1 - SSE / SST
```

Extract fit statistics:

```r
summary(m)$r.squared
summary(m)$adj.r.squared
summary(m)$fstatistic
sigma(m)                    # residual standard error
```

The residual standard error and adjusted $R^2$ are

$$
s=\sqrt{\frac{\text{SSE}}{n-k-1}},
\qquad
R^2_{\text{adjusted}}
=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-k-1}.
$$

For $k$ slopes,

$$
F=\frac{\text{SSR}/k}{\text{SSE}/(n-k-1)}
$$

tests

$$
H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_k=0
$$

against the alternative that at least one slope is not zero. Read F as the
explained variation per predictor, divided by the residual variation per
residual degree of freedom. In simple regression, the overall $F$ statistic
equals the square of the t statistic of the slope. $R^2$ is the share of
the variation in this sample that the model explains. It is not evidence of
causation, and it does not show how well the model predicts new data.

Robust standard errors and robust 95% confidence intervals
([Lecture 3](i03-inference-fit-ftest.qmd#i03-robust)):

```r
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

coeftest(m, vcov. = vcovHC(m, type = "HC1"))
coefci(m, vcov. = vcovHC(m, type = "HC1"))
```

Robust standard errors remain valid when the error variance is not
constant. They do not repair a wrong shape of the model, they do not remove
confounding, and they do not make a coefficient causal.

## Lecture 4: Multiple linear regression

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kX_{ik}+\varepsilon_i.
$$

```r
m_multi <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = analysis)
summary(m_multi)
confint(m_multi)
```

Interpret $\hat\beta_j$ as the fitted change in the outcome for a one-unit
increase in $X_j$, holding the other included predictors fixed. Include:

- the estimate and its direction
- the predictor step and its unit
- the unit of the outcome
- the predictors that are held fixed
- the analysed sample, and "associated with" unless the data come from an
  experiment.

For changes $\Delta x_1,\ldots,\Delta x_k$, the additive fitted difference
is

$$
\Delta\widehat Y=\hat\beta_1\Delta x_1+\cdots+\hat\beta_k\Delta x_k.
$$

Use `predict()` to combine terms without manual arithmetic:

```r
cases <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(x1_A, x1_B),
  x2 = c(x2_A, x2_B),
  x3 = c(x3_A, x3_B)
)
fits <- predict(m_multi, newdata = cases)
fits[2] - fits[1]
```

A regression table with one column per model, as in a research paper. You
need this for your thesis, not at the exam. Install the package once with
`install.packages("modelsummary")`. All models must use the same
observations:

```r
library(modelsummary)
m_a <- lm(y ~ x1, data = analysis)
m_b <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = analysis)
modelsummary(
  list("(1)" = m_a, "(2)" = m_b, "(3)" = m_multi),
  stars = c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared")
)
```

`modelsummary` rounds to three decimals.

## Lecture 5: Factors, reference categories, and partial F-tests

Set a reference category before fitting:

```r
analysis$group <- relevel(factor(analysis$group), ref = "reference")

m_group <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + group, data = analysis)
summary(m_group)
coef(m_group)
confint(m_group)
```

Each printed group coefficient compares that category with the reference
category, holding the other included predictors fixed. Releveling changes
which comparisons are reported. It does not change the fitted values:

```r
analysis$group_alt <- relevel(analysis$group, ref = "other")
m_alt <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + group_alt, data = analysis)
all.equal(fitted(m_group), fitted(m_alt))
```

Compare nested models fitted to the same observations:

```r
reduced <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = analysis)
complete <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + group, data = analysis)
anova(reduced, complete)
```

The partial F-test asks whether the coefficients of all terms that are left
out of the reduced model are zero at the same time. The reduced model must
be the complete model without some of its terms, and both models must use
the same outcome and the same observations.

If the complete model has $k_C$ slopes and the reduced model leaves out $q$
of these terms,

$$
F=
\frac{(\text{SSE}_{R}-\text{SSE}_{C})/q}
{\text{SSE}_{C}/(n-k_C-1)}.
$$

## Lecture 6: Interactions and polynomial terms

For an interaction between a numerical predictor $X$ and a dummy $D$,

$$
\widehat Y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X+\hat\beta_2D+\hat\beta_3XD.
$$

- $D=0$: intercept $\hat\beta_0$, slope $\hat\beta_1$
- $D=1$: intercept $\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_2$, slope $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_3$
- $\hat\beta_3$: difference in slopes.

Use `*` to include $X$, $D$, and their interaction (the hierarchy
principle):

```r
m_interaction <- lm(y ~ x * group + z, data = analysis)
# x * group expands to x + group + x:group
summary(m_interaction)
```

Centering (subtracting the mean) changes the meaning of the intercept and
of the group coefficient. It does not change the fitted values or the
interaction estimate:

```r
analysis$x_c <- analysis$x - mean(analysis$x)
m_centered <- lm(y ~ x_c * group + z, data = analysis)
```

For a quadratic model,

$$
\widehat Y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X+\hat\beta_2X^2,
$$

the change from $x$ to $x+1$ is $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)$, and more generally the
fitted change from $x_A$ to $x_B$ is

$$
\Delta\widehat Y
=\hat\beta_1(x_B-x_A)+\hat\beta_2(x_B^2-x_A^2).
$$

```r
m_linear <- lm(y ~ x + z, data = analysis)
m_quadratic <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2) + z, data = analysis)

summary(m_quadratic)
anova(m_linear, m_quadratic)
```

`I(x^2)` tells R to calculate the square. Keep the term $x$ in the model,
never interpret $\hat\beta_1$ alone while $x^2$ is in the model, and do not
use the curve beyond the observed range of $x$.

Create fitted values for a graph:

```r
grid <- expand.grid(
  x = seq(min(analysis$x), max(analysis$x), length.out = 100),
  group = levels(analysis$group),
  z = mean(analysis$z)
)

pred <- predict(m_interaction, newdata = grid, interval = "confidence")
plot_data <- cbind(grid, pred)
```

## Commands by purpose

| Purpose | R command |
|---|---|
| Fit a model | `lm(y ~ predictors, data = df)` |
| Full model output | `summary(m)` |
| Coefficients only | `coef(m)` |
| 95% coefficient intervals | `confint(m)` |
| Fitted values and residuals | `fitted(m)`, `residuals(m)` |
| Summary of the residuals | `summary(residuals(m))` |
| Standardised residuals | `rstandard(m)` |
| Influence | `cooks.distance(m)` |
| Fitted values for new cases | `predict(m, newdata = ..., interval = "confidence")` |
| $R^2$, adjusted $R^2$, overall F | `summary(m)` |
| Residual degrees of freedom | `df.residual(m)` |
| Multiplier for a 95% interval | `qt(0.975, df.residual(m))` |
| Partial F-test of nested models | `anova(reduced, complete)` |
| Set the reference category of a factor | `relevel(factor(x), ref = "category")` |
| Interaction | `x * z` |
| Square in a formula | `I(x^2)` |
| Regression table with several models (thesis) | `modelsummary(list(...))` |

:::

violations of the assumptions, consult
